t.1.44.2: Then that best of serpents, having heard this exceedingly unwelcome news, spoke to his dejected sister, himself even more dejected.
t.1.44.1: The Sūta said: As soon as her husband had gone, O you whose wealth is austerity, Jaratkāru quickly went to her brother and told him of her husband's departure exactly as it had happened.
t.1.44.4: "That mighty one, it is said, will free us from the snake sacrifice; thus did the Grandfather, together with the gods, tell me long ago."
t.1.44.3: You know, good lady, what was to be accomplished and what the reason was for giving you in marriage: that, for the welfare of the serpents, a son of yours might come from him.
t.1.44.5: Fortunate lady, is there a child in your womb from that best of sages? For I do not wish that wise man's act of taking a wife to be fruitless.
t.1.44.6: Admittedly it is not proper for me to question you about such a matter, but because the matter is of such great weight, I have pressed you.
t.1.44.7: Knowing the irascible temper of your husband, an ascetic of surpassing austerity, I will not go after him, for he might perhaps curse me.
t.1.44.9: Thus addressed, Jaratkāru then spoke these words in reply, comforting the anguished Vāsuki, lord of the serpents.
t.1.44.8: Tell me, good lady, everything that your husband did. Pull out, good lady, the terrible dart that has long been lodged in my heart.
t.1.44.10: I asked that great-souled ascetic of great austerities about offspring, and pointing to this womb of mine, he said, "There is," and then he departed.
t.1.44.12: You should feel no distress about the purpose, O serpent-woman, for a son will be born to you whose radiance equals that of blazing fire and the sun.
t.1.44.11: Even in idle talk I do not recall that he ever before spoke anything untrue; how then, O king, will he speak falsely in a matter of such grave consequence?
t.1.44.13: Having spoken thus to me, brother, my husband went away to the ascetics' forest. Therefore let this great sorrow that dwells in your mind depart.
t.1.44.15: With words of comfort, marks of respect, and gifts of wealth, and with worship befitting her, the foremost of serpents honored his sister, born of the same womb.
t.1.44.14: Having heard this, Vāsuki, the lord of the Nāgas, with supreme joy accepted those words of his sister, saying, "So be it."
t.1.44.16: Then that embryo, of great splendor and radiant as the sun, grew, O best of the twice-born, just as the moon risen in the sky grows during the bright fortnight.
t.1.44.17: Then in due time, O Brahmin, she, the sister of the serpent, gave birth to a boy resembling a child of the gods, a dispeller of the fear of his father's and mother's lines.
t.1.44.18: And he grew up right there in the dwelling of the king of the Nāgas, and he learned the Vedas together with their auxiliary limbs from the Bhārgava, the son of Cyavana.
t.1.44.19: Even as a mere boy he had observed his vows and was endowed with intelligence, courage and virtue; and his name became famous in the worlds as Āstīka.
t.1.44.21: Even as a boy, living and moving about there in the house of the king of serpents, he of boundless intelligence was carefully protected.
t.1.44.20: Because his father said “He is” and went away to the forest while he was still in the womb, this name of his became renowned as Āstīka.
t.1.44.22: Like the blessed lord of the gods, the trident-wielding giver of gold, he, as he grew, gladdened all those serpents.
